module_title: Harvesting Fodder at the Right Time

lessons.title: Determining the Best Harvest Stage for Hay Crops
lessons.body:
For hay, the best time to cut is when the crop has the most feed value and will dry quickly. Most grasses like Rhodes, Napier, or Brachiaria should be cut at the early heading stage, just before the seed heads fully emerge. At this stage, protein is high, fiber is digestible, and the stems are not too thick. If you wait until seeds are mature, the hay becomes stemmy and low in protein. For legumes like lucerne or desmodium, cut when 10% of the plants are flowering. This balances yield and quality. Cutting too early gives a very watery crop that is hard to dry. Cutting too late gives tough, woody stems that animals refuse to eat.

In Africa, timing also depends on the rains. You want at least 3-5 dry days after cutting. If you cut when rain is coming, the hay may mold. In the highlands of Kenya or Ethiopia, cut early in the morning after the dew has dried, around 9-10 am. In hotter areas like Tanzania or Zimbabwe, cut in the late afternoon to avoid excessive moisture loss. Use a sharp machete or sickle. For small plots, cut at 5-10 cm above the ground to allow regrowth. For Napier grass, leave 10-15 cm stubble. This helps the plant recover quickly.

To test if the crop is ready, grab a handful and twist it. If it snaps easily and feels dry but still green, it's ready to cut. If it bends without breaking, it's too wet. If it crumbles, it's too dry. Aim for 60-65% moisture at cutting. After cutting, spread the grass in a thin layer in the sun to dry. Turn it every 2-3 hours for the first day. In good sun, it can dry to 15-20% moisture in 2-3 days. Then bale or store in a dry shed. Remember, hay made at the right stage will smell sweet and be leafy. Poor timing gives dusty, moldy hay that animals may reject. So plan your cutting around the weather and the plant's growth stage.

lessons.title: Determining the Best Harvest Stage for Silage Crops
lessons.body:
Silage is made from crops that are still green and moist, so the harvest stage is different from hay. The goal is to cut when the crop has maximum energy and enough moisture to ferment properly. For maize silage, the ideal stage is when the grain is at the dough stageâabout 50% of the kernels are dented and the leaves are still green. At this point, the whole plant has 30-35% dry matter, which is perfect for fermentation. If you cut too early (before tasseling), you get low yield and too much water. If you cut too late (after black layer), the stalks become woody and hard to compact.

For sorghum or millet silage, cut when the seeds are at the soft dough stage. For grasses like Napier or Rhodes, cut when they are about 1-1.2 meters tall, before they flower. For legumes like cowpea or lablab, cut when pods are half-formed. In all cases, you want the crop to be wilted to 30-35% dry matter. If it's too wet (above 70% moisture), you'll get smelly, butyric silage. If it's too dry (below 25% dry matter), it won't ferment well and may mold.

In Africa, small-scale farmers often use pit silos or trench silos. The best time to harvest is during a dry spell, so you can chop and pack without rain spoiling the crop. Cut in the morning after dew has dried. Chop the material into 1-2 cm pieces using a chaff cutter or a sharp panga. The shorter the chop, the better the compaction. Fill the silo quickly and pack it tightly to remove air. You can test dry matter by squeezing a handful: if juice runs out easily, it's too wet; if it feels crumbly, it's too dry. Aim for a firm ball that holds together but doesn't drip. After filling, seal the pit with plastic and soil. Good silage will be ready in 3-4 weeks. It should smell like vinegar or fresh bread, not like manure. Harvesting at the right stage is the key to high-quality silage that will feed your animals well.

lessons.title: Cutting Tools and Techniques for Small-Scale Farmers
lessons.body:
Choosing the right cutting tool saves time and labor. For small-scale farmers, the most common tools are the sickle, machete (panga), and scythe. A sickle is good for harvesting cereals like maize, sorghum, and millet. It has a curved blade with a serrated edge. Use it to cut stems at about 10-15 cm above the ground. A machete is better for cutting tall grasses like Napier or elephant grass. It has a straight, heavy blade. Swing it low and close to the ground for a clean cut. A scythe is used for cutting hay crops like Rhodes grass or lucerne. It has a long curved blade and a long handle. You swing it in a semi-circle, keeping the blade close to the ground. This is faster for large areas but requires practice.

Maintain your tools. A sharp blade cuts easily and reduces effort. Sharpen your sickle or machete with a file or whetstone every day before use. A dull blade bruises the plants, which can lead to poor regrowth and disease. For motorized options, a brush cutter with a metal blade can cut 1-2 hectares per day, but it's expensive. For most smallholders, hand tools are sufficient for 0.5-1 hectare.

Technique matters. For grasses, cut at the base but leave 5-10 cm stubble. This helps the plant regrow. For legumes, cut higher, about 15-20 cm, because they store energy in the lower stems. Cut in the morning after dew, but not too early when plants are wet. Wet plants are heavy and can cause fungal problems. When cutting, work in a systematic pattern: cut a swath, then move to the next. Collect the cut material immediately to avoid sun bleaching. For hay, leave it in the field to dry; for silage, chop and pack immediately. Always wear gloves and closed shoes to avoid cuts. Keep a first aid kit nearby. With practice, you can cut a quarter-acre of Napier grass in 2-3 hours with a sharp machete. Remember, a sharp tool and good technique are more important than speed.

lessons.title: Avoiding Soil Contamination During Harvest
lessons.body:
Soil contamination is a major cause of poor silage and hay quality. When soil gets mixed with the crop, it introduces harmful bacteria like clostridia, which cause butyric fermentation and spoilage. Soil also carries mold spores and dirt that reduce palatability. To avoid this, start by cutting cleanly. Set your sickle or machete to cut at least 5-10 cm above the ground. Never scrape the soil. If you cut too low, you pick up soil and stones. For hay crops, use a clean surface. If you dry hay on the ground, place it on a tarpaulin or a clean concrete slab. Never dry on bare soil, especially after rain, because mud will splash onto the hay.

For silage, contamination often happens during chopping and packing. If you chop on the ground, soil from your shoes or tools can mix in. Use a clean tarpaulin or a concrete floor for chopping. Wash your boots before entering the silo. Don't let animals walk over the harvested crop. Also, avoid harvesting when the soil is wet and muddy. If you must harvest after rain, wait until the soil drains. For pit silos, line the pit with plastic to prevent soil from the walls mixing with the silage. For bunker silos, clean the walls and floor before filling.

Another source is dirty tools. Clean your machete, sickle, and chopper after each use. Remove soil and plant sap. For hay, if you use a baler, make sure it's clean. If you store hay on the ground, put a layer of straw or wooden pallets underneath to prevent moisture and soil contact. In Africa, many farmers lose up to 30% of their silage due to soil contamination. By keeping the crop clean, you preserve nutrients and reduce waste. A simple rule: if you can see soil on the crop, it's contaminated. So take the extra time to keep your harvest clean. It pays off in better feed and healthier animals.

lessons.title: Estimating Yield and Planning Storage Needs
lessons.body:
Before you harvest, you need to know how much fodder you will get and how much storage space you need. For a small-scale farmer, this prevents waste and ensures you have enough feed for the dry season. Start by estimating yield. For grasses like Napier, a well-managed plot can produce 20-40 tonnes of fresh matter per hectare per year. For maize silage, you can expect 30-50 tonnes per hectare. For hay, yields are lower because of drying: about 5-10 tonnes of dry hay per hectare. To estimate your plot, cut a 1m x 1m square, weigh the fresh material, and multiply by 10,000 to get yield per hectare. Do this in 3-5 spots and average.

Next, calculate your storage needs. For silage, you need about 1 cubic meter of silo space per 500-700 kg of fresh chopped material. For hay, you need about 1 cubic meter per 60-80 kg of dry hay. For example, if you have 2 hectares of Napier yielding 30 tonnes per hectare, that's 60 tonnes of fresh material. If you chop and ensile, you need about 100 cubic meters of silo space (60,000 kg Ã· 600 kg/mÂ³). That's a pit 10m long, 2m wide, and 2m deep. For hay, if you dry 60 tonnes to 15 tonnes, you need about 200 cubic meters of storage (15,000 kg Ã· 75 kg/mÂ³). That's a shed 10m x 5m x 4m.

Plan for losses. Expect 10-20% loss in storage. So add 20% to your calculations. Also, consider your animals' needs. A mature cow eats about 2-3% of its body weight in dry matter per day. A 400 kg cow eats 8-12 kg dry matter. For 6 months dry season, that's about 1.5-2 tonnes of hay or silage per cow. So if you have 5 cows, you need 7.5-10 tonnes. Match your storage to your herd. Use a simple notebook to record yields and storage. In Africa, many farmers run out of feed because they didn't plan. By estimating yield and storage, you can avoid that.

lessons.title: Harvesting Crop Residues After Grain Harvest
lessons.body:
After harvesting maize, sorghum, millet, or rice, the stalks and leaves left in the field are valuable feed. These crop residues can be used as dry season feed, either as hay or silage. But you must harvest them correctly to maintain quality. For maize, after picking cobs, cut the stalks at 10-15 cm above the ground. You can chop them into 2-3 cm pieces and ensile them, or dry them for hay. Maize stover has about 5-7% protein and 50-60% digestibility. It's better than nothing for dry season feeding. For sorghum and millet, cut the stalks before they become too dry and brittle. If you wait too long, they lose leaves, which are the most nutritious part.

Harvest residues soon after grain harvest. Don't leave them in the field for weeks, as they lose quality and may be eaten by termites or burned. In many parts of Africa, farmers burn residues, which destroys feed and organic matter. Instead, collect and store them. For rice straw, cut at ground level, bundle, and dry. Rice straw is low in protein (3-4%) but can be treated with urea to improve digestibility. For legume residues like cowpea or groundnut haulms, these are high in protein (10-15%) and should be harvested carefully. Cut them before they dry completely, and dry them in the shade to preserve leaves.

Storage is similar to hay. Dry residues to 15-20% moisture, then store in a dry shed or stack covered with plastic. For silage, chop and pack into a pit, adding water if too dry. You can mix maize stover with legume residues for better fermentation. In West Africa, farmers often stack sorghum stover on raised platforms to protect from termites and rain. In East Africa, maize stover is often left in the field for grazing, but this leads to waste. Better to harvest and store. A good practice is to harvest residues immediately after grain harvest, when they are still green and palatable. This gives you extra feed for the dry season at no extra cost. So don't burn or ignore themâthey are a valuable resource.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Harvesting Fodder at the Right Time

Every tonne of silage or hay you harvest is a business decision. Cut too early and you harvest water instead of nutrients. Cut too late and you harvest fibre your animals cannot digest. In African smallholder and emerging commercial systems, where labour is scarce, rain is unpredictable, and machinery access is limited, timing is the single highest-leverage variable in fodder economics. This practical reference gives you the decision rules, tools, and checklists to get harvest timing right â and to protect the value of the crop from field to storage.

Why Timing Drives Profit

For a small-scale farmer in Kenya, Tanzania, or Zambia, the cost of harvesting is largely fixed â labour, fuel, twine, and storage. What changes with timing is the value of what you harvest. A one-week delay can reduce crude protein by 15â25% and increase acid detergent fibre (ADF) enough to cut milk yield per cow by 1â2 litres per day. On a 10-cow dairy unit, that is 300â600 litres per month lost â often more than the entire monthly labour bill for harvesting.

Determining the Best Harvest Stage for Hay Crops

Hay is dried forage. The goal is to preserve maximum leaf and nutrient content while achieving safe storage moisture (below 15â18% in humid African climates, ideally 12â14% in drier areas). For tropical grasses such as Rhodes grass, Napier, and Brachiaria, harvest at the boot-to-early-heading stage â typically 4â6 weeks after regrowth in the rainy season.

For legumes used in hay (e.g. lucerne/alfalfa, lablab, desmodium), cut at 10% flowering. Cutting earlier gives higher protein but lower yield and slower regrowth; cutting later gives more bulk but brittle stems that shatter leaves during drying â and leaves are where the protein is.

Table 1: Recommended harvest stages for common African hay and silage crops
Crop Hay harvest stage Silage harvest stage Target DM % at harvest
Napier grass (elephant grass) Boot stage, 1.0â1.2 m, 5â6 weeks regrowth 1.0â1.5 m, 5â7 weeks Hay: 85â88%; Silage: 28â32%
Rhodes grass Early heading, 4â5 weeks Boot to early heading Hay: 85â90%; Silage: 30â35%
Brachiaria (Mulato II, Cayman) 4â5 weeks regrowth, before stem elongation 5â6 weeks Hay: 85â90%; Silage: 28â32%
Maize (fodder) Not ideal for hay Milk-to-dough stage (30â35% DM) 30â35%
Sorghum / Sudan grass Boot stage, 1.0â1.3 m Dough stage Hay: 85%; Silage: 28â32%
Lucerne (alfalfa) 10% flowering Early bud to 10% flower Hay: 85%; Silage: 35â45% (wilted)
Lablab / cowpea Pod formation Early pod Hay: 85%; Silage: 30â35%

Sources: FAO (2018), Silage and Hay Making for Smallholder Farmers; ILRI (2020), Forage Seed and Fodder Production Handbook; ACIAR (2019), Tropical Forage Management Guide.

Determining the Best Harvest Stage for Silage Crops

Silage is preserved wet forage. The target is 28â35% dry matter (DM) for most tropical grasses and maize. Too wet (below 25% DM) and you get effluent runoff, butyric fermentation, and spoiled silage. Too dry (above 40% DM) and you cannot compact it enough to exclude oxygen â mould and heating follow.

The practical field test: squeeze a handful of chopped forage. If water drips freely, it is too wet â wilt longer. If it springs back and your hand is barely moist, it is ready. For maize silage, the milk-to-dough stage (when the kernel is between milky and doughy) is the standard. For grasses, the boot stage is ideal.

Cutting Tools and Techniques for Small-Scale Farmers

Most African smallholders harvest with hand tools. The choice matters for speed, labour cost, and regrowth.

Table 2: Cutting tools â cost, output, and best use for small-scale fodder harvest
Tool Typical cost (USD) Output (tonnes/day, 1 worker) Best for Limitations
Sickle (serrated) 2â5 0.5â1.0 Grasses, cereals, residues Slow; requires sharpening 2â3Ã/day
Slashing knife / machete 3â8 0.8â1.5 Napier, maize stalks, sorghum Uneven stubble; higher labour fatigue
Rotary brush cutter (petrol) 150â350 4â8 Larger plots, Napier, Brachiaria Fuel cost; maintenance; safety risk
Drum mower (tractor-mounted) 800â2,500 15â30 Commercial hay/silage Requires tractor; not for steep terrain
Forage chopper (manual or motorised) 80â600 2â10 (chopping) Silage preparation Not a cutting tool; post-harvest only

Sources: FAO (2018); CIMMYT (2021), Mechanisation for Smallholder Forage Systems; Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO) farm survey data, 2022.

Technique rules that protect regrowth:

  • Cut at 5â10 cm above ground for grasses. Cutting lower damages the growing points and slows regrowth by 1â2 weeks.
  • For Napier, leave 10â15 cm stubble. This is the single most important rule for stand longevity.
  • Cut in the morning after dew has dried. Sugar content is highest in late afternoon, but drying is faster if cut in the morning.
  • Keep blades sharp. A blunt tool bruises and tears stems, increasing drying time and nutrient loss.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Cutting Tool Hazards

Rotary brush cutters and drum mowers cause severe lacerations and amputations. In East and Southern Africa, farm machinery injuries are a leading cause of disability among male smallholders. Always: wear steel-toed boots, leg guards, and eye protection; never cut with the blade above knee height; never remove safety guards; keep children and bystanders at least 20 metres away; and never refuel a hot engine. For hand tools, cut away from your body, never toward your legs. A sharp sickle is safer than a blunt one â it requires less force and slips less.

Avoiding Soil Contamination During Harvest

Soil in silage or hay introduces Clostridium bacteria, which cause butyric fermentation, and Listeria, which can kill livestock. It also reduces palatability and digestibility. The main sources are:

  • Cutting too low â the blade picks up soil. Keep stubble height at 5â10 cm minimum.
  • Raking or tedding on bare ground â use a tarpaulin or clean concrete slab for drying where possible.
  • Rain splash â if rain falls on cut forage, soil splashes onto the leaves. Re-rake only the top layer; discard heavily soiled material.
  • Dirty equipment â clean choppers, trailers, and silage pits before use.

On a 10-cow unit, a single contaminated silage batch can cause a 20â30% drop in intake and, in worst cases, abortion or death. The cost of prevention is a tarpaulin (USD 15â40) and a few hours of care.

Estimating Yield and Planning Storage Needs

You cannot plan storage without a yield estimate. Use a simple quadrat method:

  1. Throw a 1 m Ã 1 m quadrat (or use a 1 m stick to mark a square) in 5â10 random spots in the field.
  2. Cut all forage inside the quadrat at harvest height, weigh it fresh.
  3. Average the weights. Multiply by 10,000 to get kg per hectare fresh weight.
  4. Multiply by DM% (e.g. 0.30 for silage, 0.85 for hay) to get DM per hectare.

Storage sizing rule of thumb: 1 mÂ³ of well-compacted silage holds 500â700 kg fresh weight (150â200 kg DM). A 10-cow dairy herd eating 25 kg fresh silage per cow per day for 180 days needs about 45 tonnes fresh â roughly 70â90 mÂ³ of pit or bunker space. For hay, 1 mÂ³ of baled hay holds 80â120 kg. Plan for 10â15% storage loss.

Harvesting Crop Residues After Grain Harvest

Maize stover, sorghum stover, millet stalks, cowpea haulms, and groundnut haulms are among the most underused feed resources in Africa. They are free, already on the farm, and can carry cattle through the dry season.

  • Maize stover: harvest immediately after grain harvest. Cut at 10â15 cm, bundle, and store under shade. Urea treatment (4 kg urea in 40 litres water per 100 kg stover, sealed for 3 weeks) raises digestibility by 10â15%.
  • Sorghum and millet stover: cut before the stems dry completely; store upright in shocks to avoid termite damage.
  • Legume haulms (cowpea, groundnut): these are high-protein (12â18% CP). Harvest, dry in shade, and store separately. Do not leave them in the field to bleach in the sun.
  • Storage: keep residues off the ground on a raised platform or pallet. Termites and rodents destroy 20â40% of poorly stored residues in 3 months.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm crop stage: grasses at boot-to-heading (4â6 weeks regrowth); legumes at 10% flowering; maize at milk-to-dough for silage.
  2. Test moisture: squeeze test for silage (28â35% DM); hay must be below 15â18% before baling or stacking.
  3. Set cutting height: 5â10 cm for grasses, 10â15 cm for Napier, never below 5 cm.
  4. Check tools: sharp blades, safety guards in place, fuel and oil ready, PPE on.
  5. Prevent soil contamination: use tarpaulins, avoid raking on bare soil, clean equipment.
  6. Estimate yield with quadrat method; calculate storage volume (1 mÂ³ â 500â700 kg silage; 80â120 kg hay).
  7. Harvest residues within 1â2 weeks of grain harvest; store under shade on raised platforms.
  8. Record everything: date, field, stage, DM%, yield, storage location. This data drives next season's decisions.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Silage and Hay Making for Smallholder Farmers (2018)
  • ILRI â Forage Seed and Fodder Production Handbook (2020)
  • ACIAR â Tropical Forage Management Guide (2019)
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation Publications
  • CIMMYT â Mechanisation for Smallholder Forage Systems (2021)

quiz.q: What is the best harvest stage for hay crops like Rhodes grass?
options: A) When seeds are fully mature
B) At early heading stage, before seed heads fully emerge
C) When the plant is still very young and leafy
quiz.explanation: Early heading gives the best balance of high protein and good drying.

quiz.q: For legume hay like lucerne, when should you cut?
options: A) When 10% of plants are flowering
B) When 50% of plants are flowering
C) After all flowers have died
quiz.explanation: Cutting at 10% flowering balances yield and quality.

quiz.q: Why should you leave 10-15 cm stubble when cutting Napier grass?
options: B) To help the plant regrow quickly
C) To make the hay dry faster
quiz.explanation: Leaving stubble allows the plant to recover and regrow.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for hay at cutting?
quiz.explanation: Hay crops are cut at 60-65% moisture and then dried.

quiz.q: How can you test if hay is ready to cut?
options: A) Twist a handful; if it snaps easily, it's ready
B) If it feels wet and heavy
C) If it crumbles into powder
D) If it smells like manure
quiz.explanation: A snap test indicates the crop is at the right stage.

quiz.q: What is the ideal stage to harvest maize for silage?
options: B) At dough stage when kernels are dented
D) When stalks are completely dry
quiz.explanation: Dough stage gives the best dry matter and energy for fermentation.

quiz.q: What dry matter percentage is ideal for silage fermentation?
quiz.explanation: 30-35% dry matter ensures proper fermentation and prevents spoilage.

quiz.q: What happens if silage is too wet (above 70% moisture)?
options: B) It produces butyric acid and smells bad
quiz.explanation: Too wet silage leads to butyric fermentation and poor quality.

quiz.q: How can you test dry matter for silage?
options: A) Squeeze a handful; if juice runs out easily, it's too wet
B) If it feels crumbly, it's too dry
quiz.explanation: The squeeze test helps judge if moisture is too high or too low.

quiz.q: What is the ideal chop length for silage?
quiz.explanation: Short chop improves compaction and fermentation.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for cutting tall grasses like Napier?
quiz.explanation: A machete is heavy and straight, ideal for tall grasses.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of a scythe over a machete for hay crops?
options: B) It cuts faster over large areas
C) It is easier to sharpen
quiz.explanation: A scythe allows faster cutting of large areas of hay.

quiz.q: Why should you sharpen your cutting tools daily?
options: A) To make them last longer
B) To reduce effort and bruising of plants
C) To cut deeper into the soil
quiz.explanation: Sharp tools cut cleanly and reduce plant damage.

quiz.q: What stubble height is recommended for cutting grasses?
quiz.explanation: 5-10 cm stubble allows regrowth without soil contamination.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid cutting when plants are wet with dew?
options: A) It is harder to cut
B) It can cause fungal problems
D) It makes the hay too dry
quiz.explanation: Wet plants are more prone to fungal growth during drying.

quiz.q: What is a major cause of poor silage quality?
quiz.explanation: Soil introduces harmful bacteria that cause spoilage.

quiz.q: How can you avoid soil contamination during hay drying?
options: B) Dry on a tarpaulin or concrete slab
quiz.explanation: A clean surface prevents soil from mixing with hay.

quiz.q: Why should you clean your tools before chopping silage?
options: A) To prevent soil and mold contamination
B) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: Dirty tools can introduce soil and spoilage organisms.

quiz.q: How much silage loss can occur due to soil contamination?
quiz.explanation: Soil contamination can cause up to 30% loss in silage quality.

quiz.q: What is a simple rule to check for soil contamination?
options: A) If you can see soil on the crop, it's contaminated
B) If it smells sweet, it's clean
C) If it's green, it's clean
D) If it's dry, it's clean
quiz.explanation: Visible soil indicates contamination and risk of spoilage.

quiz.q: What is a typical yield of fresh Napier grass per hectare per year?
quiz.explanation: Well-managed Napier can yield 20-40 tonnes fresh per hectare.

quiz.q: How much silo space is needed for 1 tonne of fresh chopped silage?
quiz.explanation: About 1.5-2 cubic meters per tonne, or 1 mÂ³ per 500-700 kg.

quiz.q: What is the daily dry matter intake of a 400 kg cow?
quiz.explanation: Cows eat about 2-3% of body weight in dry matter.

quiz.q: Why should you add 20% to storage calculations?
options: D) To store extra for friends
quiz.explanation: Storage losses of 10-20% are common, so plan extra.

quiz.q: What is the best time to harvest crop residues after grain harvest?
quiz.explanation: Harvesting soon preserves leaves and quality.

quiz.q: Which crop residue is high in protein?
quiz.explanation: Legume residues like groundnut haulms have 10-15% protein.

quiz.q: What is a common bad practice with crop residues in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Burning destroys valuable feed and organic matter.

quiz.q: How can you improve the digestibility of rice straw?
quiz.explanation: Urea treatment increases digestibility of low-quality straw.

quiz.q: What moisture content should crop residues be for storage?
quiz.explanation: 15-20% moisture prevents mold during storage.

quiz.q: Why should you store crop residues on raised platforms?
options: A) To protect from termites and rain
B) To make them easier to see
quiz.explanation: Raised platforms reduce termite damage and moisture.
